messages.subject: [stan-dev] Optimizing With Constraints
parts:
[moved to proper thread]

fabs() only gives you the right answer if you can compute what happens
when you _pass_ zero, not just when you hit zero.  This is another example
of why non-smooth objective functions break most intuition.

On Jul 18, 2014, at 6:16 AM, Bob Carpenter <notifi...@github.com> wrote:

[attempt to move to stan-dev again]

Isn't it going to be an empirical issue as to whether moving on the
squared or linear scale is more efficient?

With fabs(), don't we get the equivalent of bouncing? The derivative
is constant, it bounces us off zero back a given amount, but rather than bouncing,
we go the same amount, but switch sign. Is this even relevant?

The only problem I see with square is that it's more prone to overlflow
or underflow than the linear approach. But then that's probably not an
issue when we'll still need to be very large to overflow or very small
to underflow, and at that point, we probably have other issues.

- Bob

On Jul 18, 2014, at 1:03 AM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:

> square() or fabs() would both work and I suspect probably better than the penalty method. I would strongly suggest square() over fabs() because at least all it's derivatives exist everywhere so it's behaviour around 0 should be better.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
>
>
> On Thu, Jul 17, 2014 at 11:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> But why even both with square, why not just fabs(),
> as in:
>
> parameters {
> real sigma_signed;
> }
> transformed parameters
> real sigma;
> sigma <- fabs(sigma_signed);
> }
>
> It'd be nice if models didn't have to encode computation in
> them, but that's almost certainly unachievable without sacrificing
> efficiency.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 17, 2014, at 7:05 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > On Thursday, July 17, 2014 4:22:58 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi David. We just discussed this problem in the Stan meeting and Bob came up with a clever solution which would allow Stan to optimize on the original scale. The trick is simply to not specify the bound on beta but instead to put the constraint into the model. Something like this:
> >
> > For an optimization problem, why don't you just parameterize the likelihood in terms of squares of unrestricted primitives?
> >
> > parameters {
> > vector[K] sqrt_beta;
> > real<lower=0> sigma;
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > vector[K] beta;
> > for(k in 1:K) beta[k] <- square(sqrt_beta[k]);
> > }
> > model {
> > y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma);
> > }
> >
> > For HMC, that is a really bad idea because of the multimodal posterior but for optimization, why would it matter which mode it ended up at with respect to sqrt_beta? If there were a penalty / prior on beta, you would have to do some change-of-variables adjustments but they wouldn't be that difficult to implement.
> >
> > Ben
